lede: One characteristic, one gene, two alleles. Each parent passes on one allele, and chance decides which. A Punnett square lays out every outcome, and from it come the ratios, the test cross and the family trees the paper sets.
can: Use the genetic terms and fill a Punnett square from the parents' gametes.
Give a result as a ratio, a percentage, a probability or a number.
Work out unknown genotypes with a test cross or a pedigree diagram.

caption: One gene, two alleles, one on each chromosome of the pair. The dominant one decides the coat.

md: A **gene** controls a characteristic, and it comes in versions called **alleles**. Chromosomes come in pairs, so a body cell carries **two alleles** of each gene, one from each parent. In guinea pigs the allele **R** gives a rough coat and **r** a smooth one.

A **dominant** allele shows whenever it is present; a **recessive** allele shows only when both alleles are recessive. The **genotype** is the pair of letters: RR, Rr or rr. The **phenotype** is what you see: rough or smooth. Two alleles the same is **homozygous**; two different is **heterozygous**.

stem: A guinea pig has the genotype Rr. Give its phenotype, and the term for its genotype. [2]

steps.working: Phenotype: a rough coat.
steps.decision: R is dominant, so one R is enough for it to show.

steps.working: Genotype: heterozygous.
steps.decision: Its two alleles differ. Two alleles the same would make it homozygous, dominant or recessive.

prompt: In maize, the allele P for purple kernels is dominant to p for yellow kernels. A maize plant is pp. What is its phenotype?
options: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
explain: A recessive allele shows only when both alleles are recessive, and pp has no P to hide it, so the kernels are yellow. In the See it, Rr was rough because one dominant allele is enough.

optionNotes.why: Purple needs at least one P, the dominant allele, and this plant has none.

optionNotes.option: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
optionNotes.why: A blend would mean neither allele is dominant; here P is dominant, and with two p the kernels are simply yellow.

twin.prompt: In maize, P (purple kernels) is dominant to p (yellow kernels). A maize plant is Pp. What is its phenotype?
options: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
twin.explain: One P is enough to show, because P is dominant: a Pp plant has purple kernels.

optionNotes.why: Yellow needs two recessive alleles; the single P is dominant and shows.

optionNotes.option: a mixture of purple and yellow kernels
optionNotes.why: A dominant allele hides the recessive one completely, so there is no blend of the two colours.

md: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two chromosomes of a pair. **Meiosis** puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete, so a gamete carries **one** allele of each gene, never two. An Rr guinea pig makes R gametes and r gametes in equal numbers.

title: Why a Punnett square works
md: At fertilisation two gametes fuse, so the zygote has **two** alleles again, and mitosis copies both into every body cell. Which sperm meets which egg is down to **chance**, so every pairing of gametes is equally likely. A Punnett square's four boxes are those pairings.

stem: A guinea pig has the genotype Rr. Give the alleles its gametes can carry, and explain why each gamete carries only one. [2]

steps.working: Its gametes carry R or r, half of each.
steps.decision: One letter for each gamete. A gamete written as Rr loses the mark: it carries one allele.

steps.working: Meiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete.
steps.decision: The two alleles are on the two chromosomes of a pair, so they go to different gametes.

half carry WW and half carry ww

optionNotes.why: It tempts because Ww is the sheep's genotype, but a gamete carries only one allele of the pair.

optionNotes.why: Two letters is a genotype; gametes carry one allele each, so W or w, never a pair.

md: A **Punnett square** sets out every way the gametes can meet. Write one parent's gametes across the top and the other parent's down the side, **one allele per box**. Each inner box takes the letter above it and the letter beside it: one possible offspring.
Write each genotype with the capital letter first (Rr, never rR), then give each box its phenotype. CCEA's marks go to the square, to each parent's gametes, and to the cross being right.

stem: Two guinea pigs, Rr and rr, are crossed. Show their offspring's possible genotypes in a Punnett square. [4]

steps.working: Draw a square of four boxes.
steps.decision: The square earns its own mark before any letters go in.

steps.working: Across the top, the Rr parent's gametes: R and r.
steps.decision: One allele per box: the parent's two alleles split.

steps.working: Down the side, the rr parent's gametes: r and r.
steps.decision: A homozygous parent still makes two gametes, both the same.

steps.working: Fill the boxes: Rr, rr, Rr, rr.
steps.decision: Each box takes the letter above and the letter beside it; capital first.

title: GCSE Biology - Genetic Diagrams | Punett Squares (2027/28 exams)
why: A second run through filling the square, beside the worked steps.

prompt: Two maize plants, both Pp, are crossed. Which genotypes do their offspring have, box by box?
explain: Each parent gives P or p, so P and p go across the top and down the side. The boxes are then PP, Pp, Pp and pp. The See it filled Rr × rr the same way.

optionNotes.why: Every box Pp would need one parent to give only P and the other only p; both parents here make P and p gametes.
It pairs P with P and p with p only; each box takes one letter from the top and one from the side.

twin.prompt: Two guinea pigs, RR and rr, are crossed. Which genotypes do their pups have, box by box?
twin.explain: The RR parent gives only R and the rr parent only r, so every box is Rr.

optionNotes.why: That is the square for two Rr parents; here each parent makes only one kind of gamete.
Each box takes one letter from each parent, so it can never be RR or rr here.

md: Each parent passes on either allele with an equal chance, a half. An rr pup needs r from **both** Rr parents: a half times a half, **¼**. RR is also ¼, and Rr is **½**, because it can happen two ways.
So two heterozygous parents give genotypes **1 : 2 : 1** and phenotypes **3 : 1**, because RR and Rr look alike. A heterozygous parent crossed with a homozygous recessive one gives **1 : 1**.

stem: Show that a cross between two heterozygous guinea pigs gives rough and smooth offspring in the ratio 3 : 1. [3]

steps.working: Each parent gives R or r, each with a chance of ½.
steps.decision: Meiosis puts each allele into half the gametes.

steps.working: rr: ½ × ½ = ¼. RR: ¼. Rr: ¼ + ¼ = ½.
steps.decision: Rr arises two ways: R from the father or R from the mother.

steps.working: Rough (RR or Rr): ¼ + ½ = ¾. Smooth: ¼. So 3 : 1.
steps.decision: Three quarters to one quarter is three to one.

prompt: Two maize plants, both Pp, are crossed. Out of every 4 offspring, how many are expected to be heterozygous?
explain: Pp arises two ways, P from either parent, so it is ½ of the offspring: 2 out of every 4. The See it found Rr a half for two Rr guinea pigs.

twin.prompt: Two maize plants, both Pp, are crossed. Out of every 4 offspring, how many are expected to have purple kernels?
twin.explain: Purple is PP or Pp: ¼ + ½ = ¾, so 3 out of every 4.

caption: One square, several answers. The question decides which form to give.

md: The square gives four boxes; the question decides the form. **Ratio**: the numbers in the order the question names the phenotypes. **Percentage**: boxes out of 4, times 100. **Probability**: 1 in 4, ¼ or 0.25. **Expected number**: the fraction times the number of offspring.

Real counts rarely match the expected number exactly, because fertilisation is random. Two traps cost marks: a ratio written backwards, and a genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) given where a phenotype ratio was asked.

stem: In cats, short hair (S) is dominant to long hair (s). An Ss cat and an ss cat have 36 kittens. How many are expected to have long hair? [2]

steps.working: Square: Ss, ss, Ss, ss. Long hair is ss: 2 boxes in 4, a half.
steps.decision: Fill the square first, then count the boxes the question is about.

steps.working: 36 × ½ = 18 kittens.
steps.decision: The fraction times the number of offspring. The real count may differ a little, by chance.

md: Many marks are lost on the first line: a wrong genotype for a parent. Read every clue first. An offspring with the **recessive** phenotype is homozygous recessive, so it took a recessive allele from **each** parent.

A parent with the dominant phenotype and a recessive offspring must therefore be **heterozygous**. A parent with the recessive phenotype can only be homozygous recessive. Only when nothing points to a hidden recessive allele does a dominant parent stay 'either'.

steps.working: The black lamb is ww.
steps.decision: Black is recessive, so it shows only with two w.

steps.working: It took one w from each parent.
steps.decision: A lamb gets one allele from each parent.

steps.working: Both parents are white, so each also has a W: both are Ww.
steps.decision: Each has one w to give and one W to show.

optionNotes.why: An RR parent has no r to give, and the smooth pup needed one from each parent.

md: **Higher tier.** A rough guinea pig could be RR or Rr; looking cannot tell you which. A **test (back) cross** finds out: cross it with a **homozygous recessive** partner, a smooth guinea pig, rr, whose gametes all carry r.

Draw **two** squares, one for each genotype the unknown could have. If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, the unknown is **heterozygous**; if all show the dominant one, it is **homozygous dominant**. A description earns its marks for the partner and for what each result shows.

stem: A breeder has a rough guinea pig of unknown genotype. Describe how a test (back) cross would show its genotype. [3]

steps.working: Cross it with a smooth guinea pig, rr.
steps.decision: Its gametes all carry r, so each pup's coat shows which allele the unknown gave.

steps.working: If any pups are smooth, the unknown is Rr.
steps.decision: A smooth pup is rr, so it took an r from the unknown.

steps.working: If all the pups are rough, the unknown is RR.
steps.decision: With many pups and no smooth one, a hidden r is very unlikely.

prompt: A purple maize plant is test-crossed with a yellow (pp) plant, and all 60 of the offspring have purple kernels. What is the purple plant's most likely genotype?
explain: A Pp plant would pass p to about half its offspring, and those would be yellow. With no yellow in 60, the purple plant is almost certainly PP. In the See it, all rough pups pointed to RR.

optionNotes.why: A Pp parent crossed with pp gives yellow kernels in about half the offspring; none appeared in 60.
A pp plant has yellow kernels itself; this one is purple.

twin.prompt: A purple maize plant is test-crossed with a pp plant, and 31 of the 60 offspring have yellow kernels. What is the purple plant's genotype?
twin.explain: Each yellow offspring is pp and took a p from the purple parent, so that parent is Pp.

optionNotes.why: A PP parent has no p to give, so it could not have yellow offspring.
pp would give yellow kernels; this parent is purple.

md: **Higher tier.** In a pedigree, squares are males, circles are females, and the key says what the shading means. Here T (taster) is dominant to t, and shaded symbols are non-tasters: the **recessive** phenotype.

Start with the shaded symbols: each is **tt**. Then their parents: each passed on a t, so a taster parent of a non-taster is **Tt**. Then the children of a shaded parent: they carry a t too. Anyone left unfixed is 'TT or Tt', and saying so is the answer.

stem: The pedigree shows the ability to taste a bitter chemical in one family. T (taster) is dominant to t (non-taster). Give the genotype of individual 5 and explain how the pedigree shows it. [3]

steps.working: Individual 7 is a non-taster: tt.
steps.decision: Shaded first: the recessive phenotype has only one genotype.

steps.working: 7 took a t from each parent, 3 and 5.
steps.decision: A child gets one allele from each parent.

steps.working: 5 is a taster, so he also carries a T: Tt.
steps.decision: One t to give, one T to show.

prompt: In the tasting pedigree, individuals 1 and 2 are tasters and their daughter 3 is a non-taster. What one word describes the genotype of individual 1?
explain: Heterozygous. Individual 3 is tt and took a t from each parent, so individual 1 carries a t as well as the T that makes him a taster. The See it reasoned the same way from individual 7 to 5.

twin.prompt: In the tasting pedigree, individual 7 is a non-taster. What two words describe the genotype of individual 7?
twin.explain: Homozygous recessive: a non-taster shows the recessive phenotype, which needs two t alleles, tt.

md: **Higher tier.** When the key shades the **dominant** phenotype, start the other way round. Here freckles (F) are dominant to no freckles (f), so the **clear** symbols show the recessive phenotype: each is **ff**.

Two shaded parents with a clear child must both be **Ff**: the child took an f from each. Two clear parents can only pass on f, so all their children are ff: the chance of a child with the dominant trait is **zero**.

stem: In this family, freckles (F) are dominant to no freckles (f). Give the genotypes of individuals 1 and 2, and explain how the pedigree shows them. [3]

steps.working: Individual 3 has no freckles: ff.
steps.decision: Clear is the recessive phenotype here, so it has one genotype.

steps.working: 3 took an f from each parent, 1 and 2.
steps.decision: One allele from each parent.

steps.working: 1 and 2 both have freckles, so each also has an F: both Ff.
steps.decision: One f to give, one F to show.

prompt: In the freckles family, individual 7, who has no freckles, has a child with a partner who has no freckles. What is the percentage chance that the child has freckles?
explain: Without freckles, both parents are ff and can only pass on f, so every child is ff: a 0 per cent chance of freckles. The See it found ff for the clear individual 3 the same way.

twin.prompt: In the freckles family, individuals 4 (Ff) and 5 (ff) are expecting a third child. Give the percentage chance that this baby has freckles.
twin.explain: Ff × ff gives Ff, Ff, ff, ff: 2 boxes in 4 have an F, a 50 per cent chance.

md: **The two-generation diagram** (2025). Circles to fill row by row: parents, gametes, first generation, their gametes, second generation. One letter per gamete circle.
**Choose the square** (2024). Finished squares with their gametes hidden: work the cross yourself first, then find the square that matches.
**A new pair of parents** (2023). When part (b) names its own parents, use those, never the pair from part (a).
**Draw two squares** (2022). A parent with the dominant phenotype and an unknown genotype needs two squares, one for each genotype it could have.

stem: In maize, purple kernels (P) are dominant to yellow (p). A PP plant is crossed with a pp plant, and two of their offspring are then crossed. Give the genotypes in each row of the diagram. [4]

steps.working: Parents PP and pp; their gametes P and p.
steps.decision: A homozygous parent makes only one kind of gamete.

steps.working: First generation: Pp and Pp, all purple.
steps.decision: Each offspring takes P from one parent and p from the other.

steps.working: Each first-generation plant's gametes: P and p.
steps.decision: Now both parents are heterozygous, so each makes two kinds.

steps.working: Second generation: PP, Pp, Pp, pp.
steps.decision: Three purple to one yellow reappears in the second generation.

prompt: A homozygous rough guinea pig (RR) is crossed with a smooth one (rr), and two of their pups are then crossed. Out of every four second-generation pups, how many are expected to be smooth?
explain: Every first-generation pup is Rr, so the second cross is Rr × Rr: one box in four is rr, smooth. The maize diagram in the See it gave one yellow in four the same way.

optionNotes.why: That is true of the first generation, all Rr; crossing two of them brings rr back in one box of four.
Two in four comes from Rr × rr; the second generation here comes from Rr × Rr.

twin.prompt: A homozygous rough guinea pig (RR) is crossed with a smooth one (rr). Out of every four of their pups, the first generation, how many are smooth?
twin.explain: Every pup takes R from the RR parent and r from the rr parent: all Rr, all rough.

optionNotes.why: One in four is the second generation, from Rr × Rr; the first generation is all Rr.
Half smooth would need an Rr parent; here one parent gives only R.

caption: The chain's square: fix the parents from the pedigree, then cross them.

md: The hardest version chains it: fix two parents' genotypes from the pedigree, draw their square, then give the chance of one outcome for their next child. Each child is a fresh chance, so earlier children change nothing.

title: Draw the square even when unsure
md: The square is set most years, yet in 2024 many could not complete it. A square drawn correctly from wrong gametes still earns marks, so always write the gametes and the square.

stem: In the tasting pedigree, individuals 1 and 2 are both Tt. Give the probability that a further child of theirs is heterozygous. [3]

steps.working: Gametes: T and t from each parent.
steps.decision: Both are heterozygous, so each makes two kinds of gamete.

steps.working: Square: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
steps.decision: Each box is one quarter of the chances.

steps.working: Heterozygous, Tt, is 2 boxes in 4: a probability of one half.
steps.decision: Count the boxes that match what the question asks, and only those.

prompt: Individuals 1 and 2 of the tasting pedigree are both Tt. Give the percentage chance that a further child of theirs is a non-taster.
explain: A non-taster is tt: 1 box in 4 of the Tt × Tt square, so 25 per cent. The See it counted the two Tt boxes; here only the tt box counts.

twin.prompt: Individuals 1 and 2 of the tasting pedigree are both Tt. Give the percentage chance that a further child of theirs is a taster.
twin.explain: A taster is TT or Tt: 3 boxes in 4, so 75 per cent.

md: A late question of seven to eleven marks, opened by a pedigree or a described cross. The first mark is usually a genotype or a term; the last is a ratio, a percentage or a test cross described in full. Stuck? Write each parent's genotype, split it into gametes, and draw the square.
